Radar Cross-Section (RCS) is defined as σ = 4πR² |Es|² / |Ei|², where Es and Ei are scattered and incident electric fields respectively.
Antennas inherently increase RCS due to their metallic geometry and radiating nature.
Three antenna models were designed: baseline (Model A), geometrically optimized (Model B), and hybrid with RAM and FSS (Model C).
Model A operates with a resonant frequency at 3.9 GHz and a -10 dB bandwidth of 3.1–4.8 GHz.
Model B's geometric modifications shifted resonance to 4.2 GHz and expanded bandwidth to 3.8–6.0 GHz.
Model C, integrating RAM and FSS, achieved a bandwidth of 3.5–7.8 GHz with return loss below -10 dB.
Model A showed a peak RCS of about +3 dBsm at 5 GHz.
Model B reduced RCS to approximately -8 dBsm in the 4–8 GHz range.
Model C achieved a minimum RCS of -15 dBsm at 5 GHz, representing an 80% reduction compared to Model A.
FSS selectively reflects or transmits electromagnetic waves to reduce backscatter outside the operating band.
RAM absorbs incident radar waves, converting electromagnetic energy into heat, reducing reflections.
Geometric shaping such as edge serration and curvature disrupts surface currents and scatters radar waves directionally.
The hybrid antenna maintained constant gain and directivity despite a slight decrease in radiation efficiency.
CST Microwave Studio was used for electromagnetic simulation and optimization of antenna designs.
The study covers a wide frequency range (2–12 GHz), relevant for satellite communication, radar, Wi-Fi, and microwave relays.
Return loss (S11) below -10 dB indicates good impedance matching and efficient radiation.
Surface current distribution analysis is key to understanding and controlling antenna scattering behavior.
Active and reconfigurable RCS control techniques involve tunable materials and electronic components but were not the focus here.
The combined use of geometric shaping, RAM, and FSS provides a synergistic effect in RCS reduction.
The study provides a foundation for future research into metamaterials and machine learning for adaptive RCS control.
